Demoralize

dih-MOR-uh-lyz · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To demoralize is to drain someone of confidence, hope, or discipline.

A string of careless blunders in the final round left the chess player thoroughly demoralized, doubting every move he made afterward.

Worked Example

Weeks of grim news from home demoralized the soldiers long before the battle even began.

The soldiers weren't physically weaker -- their spirit and resolve had been worn down, which is exactly what demoralize describes.

How Demoralize Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

dishearten

dishearten: to cause someone to lose hope or enthusiasm

discourage

discourage: to cause someone to lose confidence or enthusiasm

Antonyms

encourage

encourage: to give someone confidence or hope

embolden

embolden: to give someone the courage to do something

How Strong Is It? — unsettle → demoralize → crush

unsettle vs. demoralize

unsettle vs. demoralize: To unsettle someone is to make them mildly uneasy, less severe than draining their confidence entirely.

crush vs. demoralize

crush vs. demoralize: To crush someone's spirit is to destroy their confidence completely, an even more total blow than demoralize.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — de-

prefix — de-: removal of (Latin)

root — moral

root — moral: having to do with character, spirit, or confidence (Latin moralis, via French)

suffix — -ize

suffix — -ize: to make, to cause to be (Greek)

Put it together

Put it together: Demoralize combines de- ('removal of') with the everyday word moral -- here in the sense of morale, a group's shared spirit and confidence -- plus -ize, 'to make happen.' To demoralize someone is literally to strip away their morale.

Use the root in a new word: morale

Use the root in a new word: morale: The coach worked hard to keep team morale high even after a tough loss.

Root Check

Word Choice

Demoralize describes a drop in confidence or spirit, not a physical injury -- it's most often used about teams, soldiers, workers, or students facing repeated setbacks.
